analysis.one_liner: Ends federal subsidies, tax breaks, and royalty discounts for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2020 with zero cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip away a long list of special benefits that oil, natural gas, and coal companies get from the federal government: tax deductions and credits written for drillers and miners, sweetheart royalty rates on federal land, a government research program for fossil energy, and public financing for fossil fuel projects abroad. It would also block fossil fuel companies from tapping pandemic business-relief loans, raise federal royalty rates from 12.5% to 18.75%, lift caps on what companies must pay after oil spills, and make tar sands, coal liquids, and oil shale subject to the petroleum excise tax that funds oil spill cleanup.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop footing the bill for industry-specific tax breaks and research spending; communities and coastlines exposed to oil spills, because liability caps would be lifted and the spill-cleanup fund would collect more; and cleaner energy producers, who would no longer compete against companies enjoying government-funded advantages. Black lung coal miners would also gain from a permanently higher excise tax funding the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates a long list of tax provisions written specifically for fossil fuel companies, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, the marginal well credit, percentage depletion for coal, capital-gains treatment for coal royalties, and special expensing for intangible drilling costs.

Raises federal royalty rates for coal, oil, and gas leases on public land from 12.5% to 18.75%, so the public collects more when companies extract from federal land, and repeals royalty relief provisions that let companies pay less than the standard rate.

Removes the $75 million cap above insurance for offshore facility spill liability and ends caps entirely for pipelines carrying tar sands oil, meaning companies responsible for spills must pay the full cost of the damage.

Bars fossil fuel companies from pandemic-era federal loan and loan guarantee programs under the CARES Act and from the Defense Production Act, so taxpayer-backed pandemic relief cannot flow to companies that extract, transport, or refine oil, gas, and coal.

Prohibits the Export-Import Bank, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, and U.S. contributions to international financial institutions from financing fossil fuel projects, and terminates the Department of Energy's Fossil Energy Research and Development Program.

Permanently sets a higher excise tax funding the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which pays benefits to coal miners disabled by the disease, and raises the per-barrel rate funding the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund.

Expands the petroleum excise tax definition of crude oil to cover tar sands oil, liquid fuels from coal, and oil shale, closing a gap that had let those fuels escape the tax that pays for oil spill cleanup.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, natural gas, and coal companies, which would lose the tax deductions, credits, below-market royalties, federal research money, and public financing they currently receive. Some of those costs could be passed through to consumers in the form of slightly higher energy prices, and banks and large financial institutions would face new limits on financing and owning fossil fuel businesses.

drawbacks.text: The higher federal royalty rate, a new 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico production, and the loss of drilling and mining tax breaks would raise production costs, and companies could pass some of those costs to consumers as higher energy prices — an effect worth scrutiny during a pandemic recession.

The bill terminates the federal credit for carbon oxide sequestration, a technology some climate analysts view as a necessary tool for cutting emissions, because that credit also subsidizes using captured carbon to push more oil out of wells.

Eliminating special tax treatment such as intangible drilling cost expensing and last-in, first-out inventory accounting for energy firms would impose transition costs and bookkeeping burdens on those companies, including smaller producers.

The moratorium on new federal oil, gas, and coal leases during the COVID-19 national emergency and the two-year restrictions on banks connected to CARES Act programs would be broad interventions in energy markets and lending during an economic crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to the broad public — taxpayers stop paying for industry-specific tax breaks, spill victims get uncapped liability, and miners get a funded black lung program — while the costs fall on a concentrated set of companies, some of which could shift modest amounts to consumers through energy prices. The bill is sweeping and touches dozens of overlapping tax and lending rules at once, which raises the chance of unintended effects on smaller producers and on the few clean-adjacent programs (carbon capture) it cuts, but the core design is a straightforward removal of preferential treatment rather than a new subsidy scheme.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on November 10, 2020, near the end of the 116th Congress.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had no visible support beyond its sponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the panel with jurisdiction over tax provisions; that was the last action of any kind.
The Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup, the full Senate never debated it, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies are better off, because every tax break, discounted royalty, research program, and financing channel the bill targeted remained in place. Taxpayers continued paying for those benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies kept every subsidy

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2020 and read it twice on the Senate floor, where it was referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on November 10, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry lobbying groups
against.role: Industry advocates defending existing tax breaks and royalty terms
against.what_they_did: Opposed ending fossil fuel subsidies, as the industry has consistently done in response to similar proposals to strip oil, gas, and coal tax preferences.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever happened and no senator besides the sponsor signed on, so no party split was ever recorded; the bill's only visible support was an independent senator aligned with Democrats, and the committee that buried it was Republican-led.

industries.note: The bill strips their tax credits and special expensing rules, raises federal royalties from 12.5% to 18.75%, imposes a 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico production, removes oil spill liability caps, and blocks them from CARES Act pandemic loans. The industry's current arrangement keeps taxpayer support flowing while the public absorbs spill and pollution risks.

It repeals percentage depletion and capital-gains treatment for coal royalties, raises the royalty rate on federal coal leases, permanently increases the excise tax that funds black lung benefits for miners, and ends a renewable-energy credit that subsidized refined coal.

industries.industry: Tar sands, oil shale, and coal-to-liquid producers
industries.note: These fuels would be brought under the petroleum excise tax for the first time, and pipelines carrying tar sands oil would lose their liability cap, ending a favorable carve-out from the cost of spill cleanup.

Banks receiving CARES Act program benefits would be barred from taking ownership stakes in fossil fuel businesses, and lenders with $10 billion or more in assets would lose their exemption from cleanup liability under CERCLA. Community banks are exempt from the liability change.

industries.industry: Export credit and development finance beneficiaries (fossil projects abroad)
industries.note: The Export-Import Bank, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, and international financial institutions receiving U.S. contributions could no longer finance fossil fuel projects with public money.

Ending preferential treatment for fossil fuel production removes a competitive disadvantage, though the bill also cuts the carbon capture credit and the refined coal credit, which some clean-energy interests counted on.
